claim: TDP-43 is a nuclear RNA-binding protein that forms neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions in ALS and FTLD.
source: TDP-43 is a nuclear RNA-binding protein that forms neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions in two major neurodegenerative diseases, ALS and FTLD.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Tandem RNA recognition motifs of TDP-43 bind to long GU-repeats in a cooperative manner through intermolecular interactions.
source: Here, we demonstrate that tandem RNA recognition motifs of TDP-43 bind to long GU-repeats in a cooperative manner through intermolecular interactions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including ITC, EMSA, and NMR experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The cooperative binding of TDP-43 to mRNA may be critical to maintain the solubility of TDP-43 in the nucleus.
source: Moreover, using mutants whose cooperativity is impaired, we found that the cooperative binding of TDP-43 to mRNA may be critical to maintain the solubility of TDP-43 in the nucleus and the miscibility of TDP-43 in cytoplasmic stress granules.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data from mutant analysis in cells (Figures 7 and 8) and in vitro solubility assays (Figure 6).

claim: The cooperative binding of TDP-43 to mRNA may be critical to maintain the miscibility of TDP-43 in cytoplasmic stress granules.
source: Moreover, using mutants whose cooperativity is impaired, we found that the cooperative binding of TDP-43 to mRNA may be critical to maintain the solubility of TDP-43 in the nucleus and the miscibility of TDP-43 in cytoplasmic stress granules.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by cellular data showing that cooperativity-defective mutants form mRNA-poor condensates and are excluded from stress granules (Figures 7 and 8).

claim: TDP-43 was associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) pathologies.
source: Since TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), a nuclear mRNA-binding protein with a self-attracting LCD (Cao et al., 2019; Tollervey et al., 2011), was associated to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) pathologies (Neumann et al., 2006; Arai et al., 2006; Sreedharan et al., 2008; Vogler et al., 2018; Chou et al., 2018), the notion that deregulated RBP assemblies may be responsible for RBP aggregation has made its way (Li et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The majority of pathological mutations associated with TDP-43 are located in its self-adhesive C-terminal LCD.
source: In support to this, the majority of pathological mutations associated with TDP-43 are located in its self-adhesive C-terminal LCD (Van Deerlin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: TDP-43 LCD plays a critical role in the aggregation process.
source: Many structural analyses focused on pathological TDP-43 mutations have also indicated a critical role of the TDP-43 LCD in the aggregation process (Cao et al., 2019; Conicella et al., 2016; Guenther et al., 2018; Conicella et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Under physiological conditions, TDP-43 is mostly associated with nuclear RNA, considered as a negative regulator of TDP-43 condensates.
source: Under physiological conditions, TDP-43 is mostly associated with nuclear RNA, considered as a negative regulator of TDP-43 condensates (Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A high ratio of RNA/protein in the nucleus promotes dynamic and reversible higher order assemblies of RBPs such as TDP-43.
source: A high ratio of RNA/protein in the nucleus promotes dynamic and reversible higher order assemblies of RBPs such as TDP-43, while lower nuclear RNA levels causes excessive phase separation and the formation of cytotoxic aggregates (Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Lower nuclear RNA levels cause excessive phase separation and the formation of cytotoxic aggregates.
source: A high ratio of RNA/protein in the nucleus promotes dynamic and reversible higher order assemblies of RBPs such as TDP-43, while lower nuclear RNA levels causes excessive phase separation and the formation of cytotoxic aggregates (Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the nucleus, TDP-43 binds to GU-rich sequences in introns.
source: In the nucleus, TDP-43 binds to GU-rich sequences in introns (Tollervey et al., 2011; Polymenidou et al., 2011), with a high affinity through its tandem RRM domains (Lukavsky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TDP-43 binds to GU-rich sequences with a high affinity through its tandem RRM domains.
source: In the nucleus, TDP-43 binds to GU-rich sequences in introns (Tollervey et al., 2011; Polymenidou et al., 2011), with a high affinity through its tandem RRM domains (Lukavsky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Transcripts with long introns display multiple GU-rich binding sites.
source: Notably, transcripts with long introns display multiple GU-rich binding sites (Polymenidou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: TDP-43 multimerization on long GU-rich repeats may ensure the proper packaging of introns to facilitate their processing by the spliceosome.
source: TDP-43 multimerization on long GU-rich repeats may ensure the proper packaging of introns to facilitate their processing by the spliceosome (Ishiguro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents a speculative interpretation.

claim: The specific binding of TDP-43 RRM1–2 to GU-rich RNA limits TDP-43 aggregation in vitro.
source: Consistent with the notion that mRNA keeps TDP-43 in a soluble state, the specific binding of TDP-43 RRM1–2 to GU-rich RNA limits TDP-43 aggregation in vitro (French et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The pathological mutation K181E, located in the linker between RRM1 and RRM2 domains, leads to TDP-43 aggregation and to a reduced affinity for its RNA targets.
source: In addition, a pathological mutation, K181E, located in the linker between RRM1 and RRM2 domains, leads to TDP-43 aggregation and to a reduced affinity for its RNA targets (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RRM1–2 forms successive multimeric intermediates with increasing protein concentrations in the presence of 24 GT repeats.
source: However, RRM1–2 forms, abruptly and discretely, successive multimeric intermediates with increasing protein concentrations, a hallmark of a cooperative association.
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: RRM1 alone does not show a discrete binding to 24 GT repeats, suggesting a significant role of RRM2 domain to generate stable RRM1–2 multimers.
source: However, RRM1 alone, in contrast to RRM1–2, does not show a discrete binding to 24 GT repeats, suggesting a significant role of RRM2 domain to generate stable RRM1–2 multimers.
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 1c and represents an inference from the data.

claim: The ITC titration curves of RRM1–2 with 12 GT repeats display two distinct plateaus reflecting the binding of one and two proteins.
source: The ITC titration curves of RRM1–2 with 12 GT repeats display two distinct plateaus reflecting the binding of one and two proteins, while only one plateau is observed with 6 GT repeats indicating the binding of only one RRM1–2.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The enthalpy difference (ΔH) resulting from the binding of two RRM1–2 to 12 GT repeats (~−80 kcal/mol) is more than twice the ΔH value measured when only one RRM1–2 binds to 6 GT repeats (~–33 kcal/mol), indicating an energy benefit due to a cooperative binding.
source: In addition, the enthalpy difference (ΔH) resulting from the binding of two RRM1–2 to 12 GT repeats (~ −80 kcal/mol) is more than twice the ΔH value measured when only one RRM1–2 binds to 6 GT repeats (~ –33 kcal/mol), which most probably indicates an energy benefit due to a cooperative binding.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1d and represents an inference from the data.

claim: RRM1–2 binds to 12 GT repeats with a Kd1/Kd2 ratio greater than 100, characterizing a marked cooperativity.
source: Since Kd2 is significantly lower than Kd1 for RRM1–2 (Kd1/Kd2 >100, Figure 1d), RRM1–2 binds to 12 GT repeats with a higher affinity when another RRM1–2 monomer is already associated to GT repeats, which characterizes a marked cooperativity.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The ratio Kd1/Kd2 was not significantly higher for isolated RRMs, RRM1 and RRM2 fragments (Kd1/Kd2 = 8.9 and 0.05, respectively) than for RRM1–2 (Kd1/Kd2 = 128).
source: Interestingly, the ratio Kd1/Kd2 was not significantly higher for isolated RRMs, RRM1 and RRM2 fragments (Kd1/Kd2 = 8.9 and 0.05, respectively) than for RRM1–2 (Kd1/Kd2 = 128).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: A single RRM1–2 binds to 6 GU repeats mostly through conserved RNA-binding residues.
source: In agreement with the results from ITC experiments, a single RRM1–2 binds to 6 GU repeats mostly through conserved RNA-binding residues (Lukavsky et al., 2013; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2a and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Twelve GU repeats induce additional chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) and peak broadenings in RRM1–2, consistent with the binding of two RRM1–2.
source: Twelve GU repeats induce additional chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) and peak broadenings, consistent with the binding of two RRM1–2 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: CSPs observed for RRM1–2 with 12 GU repeats were specific to RRM1–2 as compared to RRM1 or RRM2 alone.
source: These effects were specific to RRM1–2 as compared to RRM1 or RRM2 alone (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Both RRM1 and RRM2 bind to RNA, despite the lower affinity of RRM2 than RRM1 for RNA.
source: Thus, both RRM1 and RRM2 bind to RNA, despite the lower affinity of RRM2 than RRM1 for RNA (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2c and represents an inference from the data.

claim: 28 residues likely critical for the homotypic interactions leading to the formation of RRM1–2 multimers in the presence of GU repeats were selected based on NMR analysis.
source: According to the above-mentioned selection rules, 28 residues likely critical for the homotypic interactions leading to the formation of RRM1–2 multimers in the presence of GU repeats were selected and represented in the RRM1–2 primary structure (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on NMR data analysis and selection criteria described in the text.

claim: Four mutations in the RRM1 sequence (T103A/S104A, K140A/T141A, T141A/G142A, and G146A) lead to a remarkable demixing between wild-type and mutant of TDP-43.
source: In RRM domains, four mutations in the RRM1 sequence, T103A/S104A, K140A/T141A, T141A/G142A, and G146A, and three mutations in the RRM2 sequence, M202A, D205A, and V220A, lead to a remarkable demixing between wild-type and mutant of TDP-43.
evidence: This is supported by microtubule bench assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Three mutations in the RRM2 sequence (M202A, D205A, and V220A) lead to a remarkable demixing between wild-type and mutant of TDP-43.
source: In RRM domains, four mutations in the RRM1 sequence, T103A/S104A, K140A/T141A, T141A/G142A, and G146A, and three mutations in the RRM2 sequence, M202A, D205A, and V220A, lead to a remarkable demixing between wild-type and mutant of TDP-43.
evidence: This is supported by microtubule bench assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Residues K140, T141, G142, and G146 are located in the long RRM1 loop 3, indicating its possible role in the liquid-liquid phase separation orchestrated by TDP-43.
source: Interestingly, the active mutations leading to a significant demixing are mostly located away from the intramolecular interface between RRM1 and 2 (Figure 3d). Indeed, residues K140, T141, G142, and G146 are located in the long RRM1 loop 3, indicating its possible role in the liquid-liquid phase separation orchestrated by TDP-43.
evidence: This is based on the location of residues identified by mutagenesis and represents an inference.

claim: The double mutant in RRM1 loop 3, T141A/G142A, strongly affects the binding of TDP-43 to 24 GT repeats as compared to wild-type and Q213A RRM1–2 proteins.
source: The double mutant in RRM1 loop 3, T141A/G142A, strongly affects the binding of TDP-43 to 24 GT repeats as compared to wild-type and Q213A RRM1–2 proteins (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: G146A has a similar affinity for GT repeats than wild-type RRM1–2.
source: RRM1–2/DNA complexes arise at similar RRM1–2 concentrations for G146A and wild-type RRM1–2, thus indicating that G146A has a similar affinity for GT repeats than wild-type RRM1–2.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4a and represents an inference from the data.

claim: G146A binds to 24 GT repeats with a reduced cooperativity compared to both wild-type RRM1–2 and Q213A mutant.
source: However, G146A binds to 24 GT repeats with a reduced cooperativity compared to both wild-type RRM1–2 and Q213A mutant.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4a and represents an inference from the data.

claim: T141A/G142A and G146A mutations significantly decrease the Kd1/Kd2 value compared to wild-type RRM1–2.
source: Accordingly, T141A/G142A and G146A mutations, but not Q213A, significantly decrease the Kd1/Kd2 value compared to wild-type RRM1–2 (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Residues M202, E206, R208, M218, and V220 display affected CSPs and/or peak broadenings when comparing T141A/G142A and G146A mutants with the wild-type RRM1–2.
source: Through the NMR spectra analysis (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we also noticed that residues M202, E206, R208, M218, and V220, all located in the same region, display affected CSPs and/or peak broadenings when comparing T141A/G142A and G146A mutants with the wild-type RRM1–2.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: SAXS analysis confirmed the formation of a complex comprising two units of RRM1–2 proteins bound to 12 GU repeats.
source: The SAXS analysis further confirmed the formation of a complex indeed comprising two units of RRM1–2 proteins bound to 12 GU repeats.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The MD model shows how the protein dimer drives and stabilizes the RNA in a configuration displaying a bend at G13 with an average bending angle of 97.5°.
source: The model shows how the protein dimer drives and stabilizes the RNA in a configuration displaying a bend at G13 with an average bending angle of 97.5° (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The calculated plot deduced from the MD model fits the experimental SAXS curve with a χ2 value of 1.28.
source: The calculated plot deduced from the MD model fits the experimental SAXS curve with a χ2 value of 1.28 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by SAXS and MD data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The MD model highlights an interaction interface created between a pocket around V220, located in the RRM2 domain of the first monomer and the RRM1 loop 3 of the second monomer.
source: This model highlights an interaction interface created between a pocket around V220, located in the RRM2 domain of the first monomer and the RRM1 loop 3 of the second monomer (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The RRM2 pocket groove is built from residues belonging to the β2 strand (M218, D219, and V220) and the α1 helix (E204, D205, and R208).
source: The RRM2 pocket groove is built from residues belonging to the β2 strand (M218, D219, and V220) and the α1 helix (E204, D205, and R208).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The RRM2 pocket of the first monomer accommodates the RRM1 loop 3 of the second monomer through several interaction pairs displaying the lowest free energy (K137-M218, K140-E204, K140-D205, T141-V220, G142-D219, and H143-D219).
source: As observed in Figure 5b (left panel), the RRM2 pocket of the first monomer accommodates the RRM1 loop 3 of the second monomer through several interaction pairs displaying the lowest free energy (K137-M218, K140-E204, K140-D205, T141-V220, G142-D219, and H143-D219) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5b and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Among the amino acid residues constituting the RRM1 loop 3, K140 and T141 contribute to ca. 65% of the total free energy provided by this loop to stabilize the interface.
source: Among the amino acid residues constituting the RRM1 loop 3, K140 and T141 contribute to ca. 65% of the total free energy provided by this loop to stabilize the interface (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: In the RRM2 pocket, E204, D219, and V220 contribute to ca. 70% of the total free energy invested in the interface by this pocket.
source: In the RRM2 pocket, E204, D219, and V220 contribute to ca. 70% of the total free energy invested in the interface by this pocket (Supplementary file 2), which is stabilized by an intramolecular network of interactions involving two residues in the β2 strand (V217 and V220) and three residues of the α1 helix (E204, L207, and R208) (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The accessibility to water of unstructured residues K137, L139, K140, H143, and G142, located in the RRM1 loop 3, was significantly affected in the dimeric state but not in the monomeric form.
source: The accessibility to water of unstructured residues K137, L139, K140, H143, and G142, located in the RRM1 loop 3, was significantly affected in the dimeric state but not in the monomeric form.
evidence: This is supported by NMR SEA-HSQC data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Residues located in the RRM2 pocket around V220, E204, M218, and V220 itself, also display reduced accessibilities to the solvent when the dimer is formed.
source: Residues located in the RRM2 pocket around V220, E204, M218, and V220 itself, also display reduced accessibilities to the solvent when the dimer is formed supporting the MD model (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by NMR SEA-HSQC data shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: A strong demixing of wild-type and mutant K137E proteins was observed.
source: However, a strong demixing of wild-type and mutant K137E proteins was observed (Figure 5d, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by microtubule bench assay data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The K137E mutant better mixed with the R208A mutant than with wild-type TDP-43.
source: Interestingly, the K137E mutant better mixed with the R208A mutant than with wild-type TDP-43 (Figure 5d, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by microtubule bench assay data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: When K140 is replaced by a glutamic acid residue (K140E mutant), no effect was observed on the mixing with either wild-type TDP-43 or R208A mutant.
source: Furthermore, when K140 is replaced by a glutamic acid residue (K140E mutant), no effect was observed on the mixing with either wild-type TDP-43 or R208A mutant, most probably because E140 is too far away from R208 in the dimeric form (Figure 5d, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by microtubule bench assay data shown in Figure 5d and represents an inference.

claim: TDP-43 at 10 μM was almost entirely found in the pellet after centrifugation, in agreement with its aggregation in the test tube.
source: We first noticed that TDP-43 at 10 μM was almost entirely found in the pellet after centrifugation, in agreement with its aggregation in the test tube (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: TDP-43 aggregates are detergent-insoluble (2% of Triton X-100).
source: These aggregates are detergent-insoluble (2% of Triton X-100).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by experimental observations.

claim: In the presence of increasing concentrations of 24 GT-repeats, a larger amount of TDP-43 was detected in the supernatant.
source: However, in the presence of increasing concentrations of 24 GT-repeats, a larger amount of TDP-43 was detected in the supernatant (three independent replicates).
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: DNase treatment of pre-incubated TDP-43/GT-repeats complexes resulted in the appearance of spherical TDP-43 aggregates by AFM and a larger amount of TDP-43 in the pellet.
source: In agreement with the critical role of GT-repeats in preserving TDP-43 solubility, DNase treatment of pre-incubated TDP-43/GT-repeats complexes resulted in the appearance of spherical TDP-43 aggregates by AFM and a larger amount of TDP-43 in the pellet.
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay and AFM data shown in Figure 6a and 6c.

claim: 6 GT-repeats that can bind only one TDP-43 monomer failed to solubilize full-length TDP-43 to the same extent as did 24 GT repeats.
source: Moreover, 6 GT-repeats that can bind only one TDP-43 monomer and 48 nt-long poly(dA) oligonucleotides for which TDP-43 has a lower affinity failed to solubilize full-length TDP-43 to the same extent as did 24 GT repeats under the same conditions (Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 48 nt-long poly(dA) oligonucleotides for which TDP-43 has a lower affinity failed to solubilize full-length TDP-43 to the same extent as did 24 GT repeats.
source: Moreover, 6 GT-repeats that can bind only one TDP-43 monomer and 48 nt-long poly(dA) oligonucleotides for which TDP-43 has a lower affinity failed to solubilize full-length TDP-43 to the same extent as did 24 GT repeats under the same conditions (Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 24 GT repeats increased the solubility of G146A but to a lesser extent than wild-type TDP-43.
source: When the solubility of G146A mutant was probed by sedimentation assays, 24 GT repeats increased the solubility of G146A but to a lesser extent than wild-type TDP-43.
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: 24 GT repeats were less potent to limit the formation of granular structures of G146A compared to wild-type TDP-43.
source: In agreement with this result, 24 GT repeats were less potent to limit the formation of granular structures of G146A compared to wild-type TDP-43 (see arrows, Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Wild-type TDP-43 and Q213A TDP-43 forms were associated to large granules enriched in mRNA.
source: Wild-type and Q213A TDP-43 forms, which bind to GU-rich repeat cooperatively, were associated to large granules enriched in mRNA (Figure 7a,b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 7a, 7b, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TDP-43-rich condensates were reversible stress granules resulting from the expression of TDP-43.
source: As these large condensates no longer appeared in the presence of cycloheximide, a stress granule inhibitor which loads ribosomes on mRNA, we concluded that TDP-43-rich condensates were reversible stress granules resulting from the expression of TDP-43.
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data and cycloheximide treatment experiments shown in Figure 7a and represents an inference.

claim: G146A and K140A/T141A form small and bright inclusions in the cytoplasm, but also in the nucleus.
source: In contrast, G146A and K140A/T141A form small and bright inclusions in the cytoplasm, but also in the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The G146A and K140A/T141A inclusions are not sensitive to cycloheximide and poorly enriched in mRNAs.
source: The G146A and K140A/T141A inclusions are not sensitive to cycloheximide and poorly enriched in mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 7a and 7b.

claim: Cycloheximide and Triton X-100 successfully dissociate stress granules, even those enriched with overexpressed wild-type TDP-43.
source: While cycloheximide and Triton X-100 successfully dissociate stress granules, even those enriched with overexpressed wild-type TDP-43, both treatments failed to dissolve nuclear and cytoplasmic aggregates of G146A mutant (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cycloheximide and Triton X-100 failed to dissolve nuclear and cytoplasmic aggregates of G146A mutant.
source: While cycloheximide and Triton X-100 successfully dissociate stress granules, even those enriched with overexpressed wild-type TDP-43, both treatments failed to dissolve nuclear and cytoplasmic aggregates of G146A mutant (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: G146A cytoplasmic condensates do not recruit other stress granules proteins, G3BP-1, HuR, and FMRP-1, in contrast to wild-type TDP-43.
source: In agreement with this results, G146A cytoplasmic condensates do not recruit other stress granules proteins, G3BP-1, HuR, and FMRP-1, in contrast to wild-type TDP-43 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sam68, a marker of nuclear stress granules (NSGs), is not recruited in nuclear G146A condensates and formed distinct Sam68 nuclear bodies (SNBs).
source: In addition, Sam68, a marker of nuclear stress granules (NSGs, Denegri et al., 2001), is not recruited in nuclear G146A condensates and formed distinct Sam68 nuclear bodies (SNBs), which means that nuclear G146A condensates cannot be considered as NSGs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: TDP-43 inclusions with G146A, K140A/T141A, and T141A/G142A mutations are mostly nuclear after hydrogen peroxide treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 8, TDP-43 inclusions with G146A, K140A/T141A, and T141A/G142A mutations are indeed mostly nuclear after hydrogen peroxide treatment (Figure 8a, b,d).
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 8a, 8b, and 8d.

claim: Even when condensates of TDP-43 mutants are not present in cells, mutations interfering with the cooperative binding of TDP-43 to mRNA still significantly reduces the shuttling of TDP-43 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: However, even when condensates of TDP-43 mutants are not present in cells, mutations interfering with the cooperative binding of TDP-43 to mRNA still significantly reduces the shuttling of TDP-43 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cellular imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The binding of RBPs to mRNA is polarized.
source: To decipher the mechanisms by which mRNA keeps TDP-43 soluble, we noticed that the binding of RBPs to mRNA is polarized (Lukavsky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the case of TDP-43, RRM1 and RRM2 bind the 5′ side and the 3′ side, respectively.
source: In the case of TDP-43, RRM1 and RRM2 bind the 5′ side and the 3′ side, respectively.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about TDP-43 structure and function.

claim: The orientation of TDP-43 ensures that consecutive N-terminal domains can hardly dimerize and that consecutive LCD domains are spatially separated to reduce multivalent interactions.
source: If we consider that multimers of TDP-43 are resulting from the concomitant and adjacent bindings of TDP-43 along mRNA, the orientation of TDP-43 therefore ensures that consecutive N-terminal domains can hardly dimerize and that consecutive LCD domains are spatially separated to reduce multivalent interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the polarized binding of TDP-43 to mRNA and the spatial arrangement of domains.

claim: Cooperativity can be essential as the binding of TDP-43 to mRNA facilitates the binding of the next TDP-43 unit nearby whereof preventing a long and flexible RNA linker between two consecutive TDP-43 to accommodate a head-to-tail TDP-43 multimer structure.
source: In addition, cooperativity can be essential as the binding of TDP-43 to mRNA facilitates the binding of the next TDP-43 unit nearby whereof preventing a long and flexible RNA linker between two consecutive TDP-43 to accommodate a head-to-tail TDP-43 multimer structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cooperative binding mechanism and its structural implications.

claim: An impaired cooperativity may promote an anarchic attachment of TDP-43 along mRNA leading to an increased occurrence of interactions between the N-terminal domains and LCDs, which may in turn promote the head-to-tail aggregation of TDP-43.
source: An impaired cooperativity may promote an anarchic attachment of TDP-43 along mRNA leading to an increased occurrence of interactions between the N-terminal domains and LCDs, which may in turn promote the head-to-tail aggregation of TDP-43.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the proposed model shown in Figure 9.

claim: The compact head-to-tail assembly leaves little room for the dynamic interaction of RRM1–2 with mRNA, which could facilitate a transition toward the formation of mRNA-poor TDP-43 condensates.
source: As the compact head-to-tail assembly leaves little room for the dynamic interaction of RRM1–2 with mRNA, a transition toward the formation of mRNA-poor TDP-43 condensates could be facilitated (Figures 9 and 8b).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the proposed model shown in Figure 9 and data in Figure 8b.
